Change control for AI agents

Agents propose changes. Current validates them, waits for your approval, applies them, and records every step in a tamper-evident log.

The Elevator Pitch · See it in action · Quickstart · How it works · Provenance · Reproducibility · Verifiability · Architecture · Intents · CLI · HTTP API · MCP · Configuration · Security · Status · Roadmap

The Elevator Pitch

Why not just use Claude Code or Codex? You can. But there, the agent acts and you approve step by step as it goes. In Current, the agent can’t act at all. It hands over a complete proposal, and nothing happens until that proposal is approved and applied.

  • Safety: The agent is limited to doing just one thing -- producing proposals. It sees only the files it asks for that Current's read policy permits, and can only propose changes from nine typed intents. Nothing touches your project until you approve it, and only allowlisted commands can run.
  • Verification: You don’t take the agent’s word for it. You review the exact proposal, or have other agents review it, before anything happens, and Current checks the agent’s claims against what actually ran.
  • Provenance: As agents write more of the code, someone will ask why was this changed, and who approved it? Current answers from a commit log: the oldest, best-tested idea in systems.

That log is hash-chained, so changes to past history are detectable, and the full state can be rebuilt from it on another machine.

Status: early. Single node, local projects. Current is not a sandbox or an authentication system: approved commands run with the runtime's privileges. See Security and the threat model.

See it in action

Ask Current to add CSRF protection to the included Next.js example:

current run "add CSRF protection to this app" \
  --dir examples/nextjs-auth \
  --model openai:gpt-5.6-sol

The model never gets the repository. It sees the layout and asks for what it needs, and Current fetches each file:

… round 1: the model asked to see 8 things
    ✓ read_file app/api/login/route.ts       769 B
    ✓ read_file lib/auth.ts                  626 B
    ✓ read_file lib/rate-limit.ts            2.4 KB
    ✓ read_file tests/login.test.ts          847 B
    ✓ read_file tests/rate-limit.test.ts     2.3 KB
    ✓ read_file package.json                 343 B
    ✓ read_file tsconfig.json                221 B
    ✓ read_file .gitignore                   83 B

Reads are confined to the project. Dependencies, build output, .git and .env* files are never shown to the model, and every read is recorded.

Then it returns a proposal:

Agent produced proposal
  proposal sha256:672c4973787b…

  The login route already invokes a missing CSRF validator before parsing
  credentials. Implement that validator with fail-closed same-origin Origin
  checking and add focused coverage for accepted and rejected origins.

PROPOSED

   1  WriteFile    lib/csrf.ts
   2  WriteFile    tests/csrf.test.ts
   3  RunCommand   npm test
   4  Report       Add fail-closed same-origin CSRF validation for the login
                   route and unit tests covering valid, absent, malformed,
                   and cross-origin headers.

✓ Proposal decoded
✓ Proposal validated

Waiting for approval. Nothing has been applied.

The agent has proposed a change. Your project is untouched.

Review the exact files and commands, or pass the machine-readable version (--json) to another agent for a second opinion:

current review sha256:672c4973787b

Then decide. Send it back with feedback, and the model reads more and returns a new proposal:

current revise sha256:672c4973787b -m "add a test for a missing Origin header"

Or approve it. Approval is recorded, but nothing runs yet:

current approve sha256:672c4973787b -m "LGTM"
✓ Approved sha256:672c4973787b
  message  LGTM

Nothing has been applied. Apply it with:
  current apply sha256:672c4973787b

Applying is its own step. Current, not the agent, writes the files and runs the command:

current apply sha256:672c4973787b
✓ Proposal approved
✓ Workflow completed

MODE: APPLY
4 effects executed.

Inspect
  current events   sha256:1429719b7546
  current proposal sha256:672c4973787b
  current artifact sha256:fb30687f1722   (raw model output)

Every step above, from the request and each file the model read to its raw reply, the approval and each effect's output, is now part of the workflow's record. current events prints it.

Quickstart

Requirements

  • Elixir 1.19 on Erlang/OTP (mise.toml pins OTP 28.5 and Elixir 1.19.5; run mise install if you use mise)
  • git, make, and bash
  • An OpenAI or Anthropic API key

1. Get the code and build

git clone https://github.com/santosh79/current.git
cd current
mix deps.get
mix compile
make client

2. Start the runtime

In one terminal, export a key and start the server. It listens on 127.0.0.1:4000 and prints every request and commit as it happens.

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="..."     # or OPENAI_API_KEY
export CURRENT_ALLOWED_COMMANDS=npm  # commands are denied unless allowlisted
bin/current-server

3. Make a request

In another terminal, from the repository root:

export PATH="$PWD:$PATH"   # puts the local `current` CLI on PATH
current models             # the models your keys give you
MODEL="openai:gpt-5.6"     # replace with a model listed above

current run "add CSRF protection to this app" \
  --dir examples/nextjs-auth \
  --model $MODEL

run stops when the proposal is waiting for review. Output varies between models and runs. Use plan instead of run for a proposal that can be reviewed but never applied.

4. Review, decide, apply

current review  <proposal-id>
current revise  <proposal-id> -m "keep the route check, add edge cases"
current approve <proposal-id> -m "reviewed"
current apply   <proposal-id>

Or current reject <proposal-id> -m "..." to end the workflow. A revision produces a new proposal ID, which must be reviewed and approved in turn; the earlier one is stale. IDs can be shortened to a unique prefix of at least four hex characters.

5. Trace it

current events   <workflow-id>   # the full chain, in log order
current proposal <proposal-id>   # intents, claims, and what the model read
current artifact <artifact-id>   # exact bytes: a file, command output, a raw reply

How it works

In a typical agent, a tool call is the action: the file is written the moment the model decides to write it. In Current, the model's output is a proposal, a list of typed intents:

"in lib/signup.ex, replace this text with that"; "run mix test"; "claim the tests pass, because that command exits 0"

A proposal does nothing on its own. Between it and your project, the runtime:

  1. decodes the model's reply, which is untrusted bytes, into a closed set of intent types. Anything outside it is rejected, not interpreted;
  2. validates it: paths confined to the project, files exist, every edit matches exactly, claims cite earlier intents they can be checked against;
  3. waits for a decision. A proposal is reviewed as a unit and approved, rejected, or sent back with feedback. The reviewer can be a person or another agent: each decision is an API call, recorded as its own event with the reviewer's metadata. A decision must name the workflow's latest proposal, and revisions are bounded (10 by default);
  4. applies it, in a separate step, with a small trusted interpreter that re-checks every path immediately before touching it and records every result;
  5. checks the outcome itself. Claims are evaluated against recorded results, and a claim that doesn't hold fails the workflow.

Every step is an event. Rounded boxes are where a workflow ends.

Producing a proposal

  1. A task is submitted with a prompt, a project directory and a model. The directory is resolved once to its real path and recorded.
  2. The model is given the project's layout: paths and sizes, no contents. Dependencies, build output, VCS directories and .env* files are left out.
  3. The model may reply with an observe request: up to 20 read_file, glob or grep intents, each with a reason. The runtime runs them read-only, under path confinement and the read policy, and asks again with the results. Up to 8 rounds, 400 KB of results in total, 200 KB per file.
  4. The model replies with a proposal. Its exact reply is stored as an artifact, whatever it contains.
  5. The proposal is decoded into typed intents (wire contract), every path is made absolute against the project, and it is validated.

Validation answers "is this well-formed and in bounds right now?", not "will it apply cleanly?". The project can change before apply, and those failures are caught and recorded then. Producing a proposal is bounded by llm_proposal_timeout_ms per call and the task's --timeout-minutes (default 10) overall.

Applying it

apply starts the interpreter. It re-checks every path against the filesystem as it is now (following symlinks), then carries out the intents in order. The first failure, or the first claim that doesn't hold, stops it and fails the workflow. Effects are not rolled back. The re-check narrows the window for a path to escape the project but doesn't close it (T2 in the threat model).

Lifecycle

created → planning → validating → waiting_for_approval
   plan mode:   → planned
   apply mode:  → approved → applying → assembling_result → completed
                → rejected
                → revision_requested → planning → validating → waiting_for_approval
                  (bounded; each pass adds a proposal to the workflow)
any stage:      → failed      (production, validation or an effect failed)
                → abandoned   (no further automatic progress is possible)
planning:  the model sees the layout, may ask to read files, then returns a proposal

Three primitives

Primitive When Role More
Intent Before execution A proposal, as data intent.md
Event After execution or decision A fact event.md
Artifact Throughout Immutable bytes, named by their SHA-256 artifact.md

Intents propose change. Artifacts hold bytes. Events record fact. State is derived from the event log.

Provenance: from a change back to the request

Because the runtime is the only thing that acts, and records each step before taking the next, every change sits at the end of an explicit chain:

TaskCreated                  the request: prompt, model, project, submitted_at
└─ WorkflowCreated
   └─ ProposalProduced       intents, what the model read first, its raw reply
      └─ ProposalValidated
         ├─ ProposalRevisionRequested   who asked for what change; loops back to
         │  └─ ProposalProductionStarted → ProposalProduced (revision 1, revises
         │     the one above) → ProposalValidated → ... up to the bound
         └─ ProposalApproved     who, when, with what message
            └─ EffectApplicationStarted
               ├─ EffectApplied      an edit: file before and after
               ├─ EffectApplied      a command: exit code, stdout, stderr
               ├─ EffectApplied      a claim: verified, and against what
               └─ WorkflowCompleted

So for any change you can answer, from the record alone and without the model:

Question Answered by
Who asked for this, and what exactly did they ask? TaskCreated: the prompt, model and project
Why does the agent say it's needed? The proposal's justification and claims
What did the model look at before deciding? Each observation, with its reason and the exact bytes it was shown
What did the model actually say? Its raw reply, stored byte for byte
Who authorized it, and when? ProposalApproved and its metadata
What did the reviewer ask to change, and what came of it? ProposalRevisionRequested and the next proposal's revision and revises
What exactly changed? Each effect's result: file before and after, command output
Did it do what the agent claimed? Each claim's verification and evidence
What didn't happen, and why? Rejections, validation failures, failed effects, each with a reason

Authorization is recorded, not enforced by identity. Current guarantees that nothing is applied without an approval event in the chain, followed by a separate apply, and the reducer enforces that at commit time. Who may approve is for a layer in front of it: approvals enter through one route (POST /v1/proposals/:id/approve), where a gateway can authenticate the caller and write verified identity into the approval's metadata. Today reviewed_by is whatever the client sends.

Reproducibility: replay the record anywhere

The commit log and the artifact store are the whole of Current's state. Nothing else is persisted, and everything the runtime shows you (tasks, proposals, workflows) is rebuilt from them. So the record is portable: copy the data directory to another machine, and replaying it gives the same history.

There are two levels of replay, and it matters which one you mean.

Replaying the record (works today). Every workflow state is a pure function of its events (see the reducer). Every piece of content those events refer to is an immutable artifact named by its SHA-256. Replaying the same log, anywhere, gives the same states, the same accepted transitions and the same rejections, and every artifact can be checked against its own name. Point CURRENT_DATA_DIR at a copy and the runtime rebuilds it on start. (Starting the runtime also resumes or fails workflows that were still in progress, which appends new events. Copy a record whose workflows have finished.)

Re-executing the proposals (planned). This is the stronger check: take the approved proposals, apply them to the same starting tree on another machine, and compare. Current records what makes that comparison exact. Each edit stores the file's before and after content hashes, and each command stores its exit code and output, so a re-run can be diffed against the original byte for byte. Edits replay deterministically. Commands are as reproducible as the environment they run in, and a difference shows up as a different artifact hash. A current export / current replay pair to do this is on the roadmap.

Verifiability: a hash-chained history

The commit log is a hash chain, the structure blockchains use to make history tamper-evident (without mining, tokens or multi-party consensus).

commit 1              commit 2                commit 3
┌────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐
│ index: 1       │    │ index: 2         │    │ index: 3         │
│ previous: nil  │◀───│ previous: H(c1)  │◀───│ previous: H(c2)  │◀── head
│ events: [...]  │    │ events: [...]    │    │ events: [...]    │
└────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘
                 H(c) = SHA-256 of term_to_binary(commit, [:deterministic])

Changing any byte of any past commit changes its hash and breaks every link after it, so the head hash fingerprints the entire history. It also covers the content: events refer to file contents, edits, command output and model replies by their SHA-256 artifact ids, so those are committed to as well.

  • Only valid successors are written. A commit must have the next index and the head's hash as previous_hash, or it is refused and nothing is written.
  • Durable before acknowledged. A commit is fsynced before anyone hears of it.
  • Verified on every start. Every link is re-checked, across segments. A gap, a broken link or corrupt bytes stop the runtime from starting, naming the file. It refuses to serve a history it can't vouch for.
  • Closed segments are immutable, and opened read-only.

Commit hashes currently use :erlang.term_to_binary/2 with the :deterministic option. This makes term encoding deterministic within the supported Erlang term format, but does not guarantee byte-for-byte identical encoding across OTP versions. Cross-version verification needs a stable, versioned canonical encoding (see the roadmap).

What this proves today: integrity. The history the runtime replays is exactly the history it wrote, unbroken and in order. What it doesn't yet: authenticity to an outsider. Commits aren't signed, so someone who can write the data directory can rewrite history and recompute every hash. Signing the head, or publishing it somewhere the writer can't reach, closes that gap: once a third party holds a head hash, every request, approval and effect beneath it is verifiable against it. That, and re-verifying artifact hashes on read, are on the roadmap.

Architecture

Current applies functional-programming and distributed-systems patterns to agent workflows. Each provides one of the properties above.

Pattern In Current Gives you
Event sourcing Every step is a typed, past-tense, versioned event. The log is the only source of truth Provenance, replay
CQRS Commands (submit, approve, revise, apply) go through Current.API and become proposed events. Queries read projections (WorkflowStore, ProposalStore, TaskStore) built from committed events Reads never mutate; writes are only events
Pure reducer WorkflowReducer.apply_event/2: state × event → state, or refusal Deterministic state; one definition of what is allowed
Immutability Events are never edited or deleted; corrections are new events. Artifacts never change A history worth verifying
Content addressing Artifacts are named by the SHA-256 of their bytes Deduplication, and content that checks itself
Hash-chained WAL Each commit carries the previous commit's hash Tamper evidence
Interpreter pattern Intents are data in a closed algebra; EffectApplicator is the one module that interprets them against the world The agent can't act; a minimal trusted surface
Pure core, impure edge Model calls and effects run at the edge and come back as events Effects are captured, not hidden
Schema evolution by upcasting Old events are migrated on read by pure, versioned functions, never rewritten on disk Old logs keep replaying through new code
Consensus interface Commits are ordered through Current.Consensus.propose/1; single-node today A path to a replicated log

The reducer

At the center is one pure function:

WorkflowReducer.apply_event(workflow | nil, event)
  :: {:ok, workflow} | {:error, {:invalid_transition, status, event_type}}

WorkflowReducer.replay(events)   # a fold of apply_event over the log

It reads no clock, touches no disk and calls no model. Every timestamp comes from the event. It is the workflow state machine, an explicit table of (status, event) → status clauses, and anything not in the table is refused:

Rule Enforced by
Nothing applies without approval EffectApplicationStarted is accepted only from :approved
A plan can never be applied ProposalApproved is accepted only for mode: :apply
One decision per proposal approval, rejection and a revision request are accepted only from :waiting_for_approval
Only the latest proposal can be decided approval, rejection, a revision request and EffectApplicationStarted must name the workflow's most recent proposal, else {:stale_proposal, given, current}
Revisions are bounded a revision request is refused with {:revision_limit_reached, max} once max_revisions (recorded on WorkflowCreated, default 10) are used
Terminal means terminal nothing moves a completed, planned, rejected, failed or abandoned workflow

The same function is used at every layer, so the layers can't disagree. EventStore replays a workflow's events plus each new one at commit time, so an event the reducer refuses never becomes canonical, and of two racing approvals only one is accepted. The API runs it as an early check before proposing. The projections are the reducer applied to the stream, and recovery replays through it on restart. Because acceptance is itself a pure function of the events already accepted, replaying the log reproduces every rejection as well as every state.

The orchestrator is a policy, not a script

WorkflowOrchestrator maps each committed event to the next event it proposes (WorkflowCreated → ProposalProductionStarted, ProposalProduced → ProposalValidated | ProposalValidationFailed, ...). It never changes state directly, and acts only on what is committed. Model calls and effects run in separate processes, and their results come back as messages that become events. Nothing an effect does counts until it is an event.

Never guess after a crash

On restart, every workflow is rebuilt from the log and resumed from what the log says. A workflow interrupted mid-apply is failed rather than resumed, because an effect that may already have happened is never repeated. One that crash-loops is retried with backoff, then abandoned on the record.

Intents

Intent What it does when applied Allowed in observe
read_file Reads a file and stores its contents yes
glob Lists files matching a relative pattern yes
grep Finds lines containing a literal string in listed files yes
write_file Creates a new file; fails if it already exists
edit_file Replaces exact text (old_string → new_string); must match once unless replace_all; stores before and after
delete_file Deletes a file; stores its contents first
run_command Runs an executable with arguments in the project; stores stdout, stderr and exit code
claim Checks a statement against an earlier intent's result (exit_code_equals, match_count_equals, match_count_greater_than)
report A summary for the reader; no effect

CLI reference

Command What it does
current run <prompt> --model <m> [--dir <d>] [--timeout-minutes <n>] Make a request; stops when the proposal waits for review.
current plan <prompt> --model <m> [--dir <d>] [--timeout-minutes <n>] Produce and validate a proposal that can never be applied.
current review <proposal-id> [--json] [--max-lines <n>] [--raw] A proposal with its edits, files and commands. --json emits current.review/v1.
current approve <proposal-id> [-m <message>] Record approval. Nothing is applied.
current reject <proposal-id> [-m <message>] Turn a proposal down; the workflow ends.
current revise <proposal-id> -m <feedback> Send a proposal back. The agent produces a replacement; follows the workflow until it waits for review again. Must name the latest proposal.
current apply <proposal-id> Apply an approved proposal, verify its claims, follow it to the end.
current events <workflow-or-task-id> The chain: a workflow's events, in log order.

--model is required; use a name current models prints. --timeout-minutes is 1 to 60. The CLI holds no state: interrupt it at any point and the workflow carries on in the runtime. Exit codes are 0 on the expected outcome, 1 on failure and 2 on a usage error.

HTTP API

The CLI does nothing a script, or another agent, can't: it calls these routes.

Route Does
POST /v1/tasks Submit a task: {"prompt", "model", "dir", "mode", "timeout_ms"} → 202 {"task_id"}
GET /v1/workflows/:id A workflow's status and events (a task id or unique prefix works)
GET /v1/workflows/:id/activity What the model has asked to see so far (?epoch=&after_seq=)
GET /v1/proposals/:id A proposal in full
GET /v1/proposals/:id/review The current.review/v1 document (?max_lines=&raw=true)
POST /v1/proposals/:id/approve Record approval: {"message", "reviewed_by"}
POST /v1/proposals/:id/reject Turn the proposal down
POST /v1/proposals/:id/revise Send it back: {"feedback", "reviewed_by"}. 409 stale_proposal if a newer proposal exists (details.current_proposal_id); 409 revision_limit_reached when none are left
POST /v1/proposals/:id/apply Start applying an approved proposal
GET /v1/artifacts/:id An artifact's exact bytes
GET /v1/models, GET /v1/health The model catalog; whether the runtime is up

Errors are {"error": {"code", "message"}} with a matching status. The API does no authentication (see Security). Every route checks Host and, when present, Origin before reading the body. Loopback Host values must use the configured runtime port; deployments behind another hostname must add its exact authority to http[:allowed_hosts].

MCP

Current also exposes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at POST /mcp, using Streamable HTTP and protocol version 2025-06-18. It exposes tools for submitting tasks, inspecting workflows and proposals, reviewing and retrieving artifacts, approving, rejecting, requesting revisions, applying proposals, listing models, and checking runtime health.

The MCP endpoint uses the same Current.API and runtime invariants as the CLI and HTTP API. Tasks return immediately with a task id; clients poll get_workflow for progress. It is stateless and tools-only: no sessions, resources, prompts, server-initiated streams, or batch requests. GET /mcp is not supported.

MCP does not authenticate callers. Anyone who can reach the endpoint can submit, approve, and apply proposals. Keep it on loopback or behind a trusted gateway that enforces access control. Like every route, it checks Host and Origin; it additionally checks MCP-Protocol-Version and Content-Type. These are not substitutes for authentication. See Security and the threat model.

Proposal snapshots. When generate_proposal_files is true, the runtime periodically writes a human-readable Markdown snapshot of each produced proposal to <data_dir>/proposals/<timestamp>-<task-slug>-<id>/r<revision>-<id>.md. They are a convenience for reading proposals outside the CLI and are regenerated from the log if missing. It is enabled in config/dev.exs and disabled by default. Snapshots can contain sensitive project content (file contents, diffs and commands), so treat them like the rest of the data directory.

Security

Current controls when an agent's proposal takes effect and records everything about it. It does not limit what an approved proposal can do.

  • Nothing an agent proposes runs without approval and a separate apply, enforced by the reducer at commit time.
  • Paths are confined to the project, checked lexically at validation and again, following symlinks, just before each effect.
  • What the model sees is filtered by name (dependencies, build output, VCS directories, .env*). Other secrets in the project are not recognised.
  • run_command is restricted by an exact executable allowlist, not sandboxed. Commands are denied by default. The proposal's cmd must exactly match a configured entry; a bare name is resolved on PATH, while a relative path containing / is resolved from the project. Allowed commands run through a Bash wrapper in the project directory with the runtime's privileges and inherited environment, including filesystem and network access. Arguments are unrestricted, so allowing interpreters, shells, package managers, or script-dispatching executables can permit arbitrary code execution. There is currently no command timeout, output-size cap, environment allowlist, or explicit descendant-process cleanup. Output is captured in unbounded temporary files until the command exits.
  • The HTTP API is unauthenticated. It listens on 127.0.0.1. Every route validates Host and browser Origin to prevent DNS rebinding, but these checks do not authenticate non-browser clients. Restrict who can reach it with a gateway, proxy or network policy; anyone who can reach it can approve and apply.
  • The log is tamper-evident to the runtime, not yet to an attacker. See Verifiability.

Full analysis: docs/threat_model.md. Please report vulnerabilities privately.

content_text: Change control for AI agents Agents propose changes. Current validates them, waits for your approval, applies them, and records every step in a tamper-evident log. The Elevator Pitch · See it in action · Quickstart · How it works · Provenance · Reproducibility · Verifiability · Architecture · Intents · CLI · HTTP API · MCP · Configuration · Security · Status · Roadmap The Elevator Pitch Why not just use Claude Code or Codex? You can. But there, the agent acts and you approve step by step as it goes. In Current, the agent can’t act at all. It hands over a complete proposal, and nothing happens until that proposal is approved and applied. Safety: The agent is limited to doing just one thing -- producing proposals. It sees only the files it asks for that Current's read policy permits, and can only propose changes from nine typed intents. Nothing touches your project until you approve it, and only allowlisted commands can run. Verification: You don’t take the agent’s word for it. You review the exact proposal, or have other agents review it, before anything happens, and Current checks the agent’s claims against what actually ran. Provenance: As agents write more of the code, someone will ask why was this changed, and who approved it? Current answers from a commit log: the oldest, best-tested idea in systems. That log is hash-chained, so changes to past history are detectable, and the full state can be rebuilt from it on another machine. Status: early. Single node, local projects. Current is not a sandbox or an authentication system: approved commands run with the runtime's privileges. See Security and the threat model. See it in action Ask Current to add CSRF protection to the included Next.js example: current run "add CSRF protection to this app" \ --dir examples/nextjs-auth \ --model openai:gpt-5.6-sol The model never gets the repository. It sees the layout and asks for what it needs, and Current fetches each file: … round 1: the model asked to see 8 things ✓ read_file app/api/login/route.ts 769 B ✓ read_file lib/auth.ts 626 B ✓ read_file lib/rate-limit.ts 2.4 KB ✓ read_file tests/login.test.ts 847 B ✓ read_file tests/rate-limit.test.ts 2.3 KB ✓ read_file package.json 343 B ✓ read_file tsconfig.json 221 B ✓ read_file .gitignore 83 B Reads are confined to the project. Dependencies, build output, .git and .env* files are never shown to the model, and every read is recorded. Then it returns a proposal: Agent produced proposal proposal sha256:672c4973787b… The login route already invokes a missing CSRF validator before parsing credentials. Implement that validator with fail-closed same-origin Origin checking and add focused coverage for accepted and rejected origins. PROPOSED 1 WriteFile lib/csrf.ts 2 WriteFile tests/csrf.test.ts 3 RunCommand npm test 4 Report Add fail-closed same-origin CSRF validation for the login route and unit tests covering valid, absent, malformed, and cross-origin headers. ✓ Proposal decoded ✓ Proposal validated Waiting for approval. Nothing has been applied. The agent has proposed a change. Your project is untouched. Review the exact files and commands, or pass the machine-readable version (--json) to another agent for a second opinion: current review sha256:672c4973787b Then decide. Send it back with feedback, and the model reads more and returns a new proposal: current revise sha256:672c4973787b -m "add a test for a missing Origin header" Or approve it. Approval is recorded, but nothing runs yet: current approve sha256:672c4973787b -m "LGTM" ✓ Approved sha256:672c4973787b message LGTM Nothing has been applied. Apply it with: current apply sha256:672c4973787b Applying is its own step. Current, not the agent, writes the files and runs the command: current apply sha256:672c4973787b ✓ Proposal approved ✓ Workflow completed MODE: APPLY 4 effects executed. Inspect current events sha256:1429719b7546 current proposal sha256:672c4973787b current artifact sha256:fb30687f1722 (raw model output) Every step above, from the request and each file the model read to its raw reply, the approval and each effect's output, is now part of the workflow's record. current events prints it. Quickstart Requirements Elixir 1.19 on Erlang/OTP (mise.toml pins OTP 28.5 and Elixir 1.19.5; run mise install if you use mise) git, make, and bash An OpenAI or Anthropic API key 1. Get the code and build git clone https://github.com/santosh79/current.git cd current mix deps.get mix compile make client 2. Start the runtime In one terminal, export a key and start the server. It listens on 127.0.0.1:4000 and prints every request and commit as it happens. export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="..." # or OPENAI_API_KEY export CURRENT_ALLOWED_COMMANDS=npm # commands are denied unless allowlisted bin/current-server 3. Make a request In another terminal, from the repository root: export PATH="$PWD:$PATH" # puts the local `current` CLI on PATH current models # the models your keys give you MODEL="openai:gpt-5.6" # replace with a model listed above current run "add CSRF protection to this app" \ --dir examples/nextjs-auth \ --model $MODEL run stops when the proposal is waiting for review. Output varies between models and runs. Use plan instead of run for a proposal that can be reviewed but never applied. 4. Review, decide, apply current review <proposal-id> current revise <proposal-id> -m "keep the route check, add edge cases" current approve <proposal-id> -m "reviewed" current apply <proposal-id> Or current reject <proposal-id> -m "..." to end the workflow. A revision produces a new proposal ID, which must be reviewed and approved in turn; the earlier one is stale. IDs can be shortened to a unique prefix of at least four hex characters. 5. Trace it current events <workflow-id> # the full chain, in log order current proposal <proposal-id> # intents, claims, and what the model read current artifact <artifact-id> # exact bytes: a file, command output, a raw reply How it works In a typical agent, a tool call is the action: the file is written the moment the model decides to write it. In Current, the model's output is a proposal, a list of typed intents: "in lib/signup.ex, replace this text with that"; "run mix test"; "claim the tests pass, because that command exits 0" A proposal does nothing on its own. Between it and your project, the runtime: decodes the model's reply, which is untrusted bytes, into a closed set of intent types. Anything outside it is rejected, not interpreted; validates it: paths confined to the project, files exist, every edit matches exactly, claims cite earlier intents they can be checked against; waits for a decision. A proposal is reviewed as a unit and approved, rejected, or sent back with feedback. The reviewer can be a person or another agent: each decision is an API call, recorded as its own event with the reviewer's metadata. A decision must name the workflow's latest proposal, and revisions are bounded (10 by default); applies it, in a separate step, with a small trusted interpreter that re-checks every path immediately before touching it and records every result; checks the outcome itself. Claims are evaluated against recorded results, and a claim that doesn't hold fails the workflow. Every step is an event. Rounded boxes are where a workflow ends. Producing a proposal A task is submitted with a prompt, a project directory and a model. The directory is resolved once to its real path and recorded. The model is given the project's layout: paths and sizes, no contents. Dependencies, build output, VCS directories and .env* files are left out. The model may reply with an observe request: up to 20 read_file, glob or grep intents, each with a reason. The runtime runs them read-only, under path confinement and the read policy, and asks again with the results. Up to 8 rounds, 400 KB of results in total, 200 KB per file. The model replies with a proposal. Its exact reply is stored as an artifact, whatever it contains. The proposal is decoded into typed intents (wire contract), every path is made absolute against the project, and it is validated. Validation answers "is this well-formed and in bounds right now?", not "will it apply cleanly?". The project can change before apply, and those failures are caught and recorded then. Producing a proposal is bounded by llm_proposal_timeout_ms per call and the task's --timeout-minutes (default 10) overall. Applying it apply starts the interpreter. It re-checks every path against the filesystem as it is now (following symlinks), then carries out the intents in order. The first failure, or the first claim that doesn't hold, stops it and fails the workflow. Effects are not rolled back. The re-check narrows the window for a path to escape the project but doesn't close it (T2 in the threat model). Lifecycle created → planning → validating → waiting_for_approval plan mode: → planned apply mode: → approved → applying → assembling_result → completed → rejected → revision_requested → planning → validating → waiting_for_approval (bounded; each pass adds a proposal to the workflow) any stage: → failed (production, validation or an effect failed) → abandoned (no further automatic progress is possible) planning: the model sees the layout, may ask to read files, then returns a proposal Three primitives Primitive When Role More Intent Before execution A proposal, as data intent.md Event After execution or decision A fact event.md Artifact Throughout Immutable bytes, named by their SHA-256 artifact.md Intents propose change. Artifacts hold bytes. Events record fact. State is derived from the event log. Provenance: from a change back to the request Because the runtime is the only thing that acts, and records each step before taking the next, every change sits at the end of an explicit chain: TaskCreated the request: prompt, model, project, submitted_at └─ WorkflowCreated └─ ProposalProduced intents, what the model read first, its raw reply └─ ProposalValidated ├─ ProposalRevisionRequested who asked for what change; loops back to │ └─ ProposalProductionStarted → ProposalProduced (revision 1, revises │ the one above) → ProposalValidated → ... up to the bound └─ ProposalApproved who, when, with what message └─ EffectApplicationStarted ├─ EffectApplied an edit: file before and after ├─ EffectApplied a command: exit code, stdout, stderr ├─ EffectApplied a claim: verified, and against what └─ WorkflowCompleted So for any change you can answer, from the record alone and without the model: Question Answered by Who asked for this, and what exactly did they ask? TaskCreated: the prompt, model and project Why does the agent say it's needed? The proposal's justification and claims What did the model look at before deciding? Each observation, with its reason and the exact bytes it was shown What did the model actually say? Its raw reply, stored byte for byte Who authorized it, and when? ProposalApproved and its metadata What did the reviewer ask to change, and what came of it? ProposalRevisionRequested and the next proposal's revision and revises What exactly changed? Each effect's result: file before and after, command output Did it do what the agent claimed? Each claim's verification and evidence What didn't happen, and why? Rejections, validation failures, failed effects, each with a reason Authorization is recorded, not enforced by identity. Current guarantees that nothing is applied without an approval event in the chain, followed by a separate apply, and the reducer enforces that at commit time. Who may approve is for a layer in front of it: approvals enter through one route (POST /v1/proposals/:id/approve), where a gateway can authenticate the caller and write verified identity into the approval's metadata. Today reviewed_by is whatever the client sends. Reproducibility: replay the record anywhere The commit log and the artifact store are the whole of Current's state. Nothing else is persisted, and everything the runtime shows you (tasks, proposals, workflows) is rebuilt from them. So the record is portable: copy the data directory to another machine, and replaying it gives the same history. There are two levels of replay, and it matters which one you mean. Replaying the record (works today). Every workflow state is a pure function of its events (see the reducer). Every piece of content those events refer to is an immutable artifact named by its SHA-256. Replaying the same log, anywhere, gives the same states, the same accepted transitions and the same rejections, and every artifact can be checked against its own name. Point CURRENT_DATA_DIR at a copy and the runtime rebuilds it on start. (Starting the runtime also resumes or fails workflows that were still in progress, which appends new events. Copy a record whose workflows have finished.) Re-executing the proposals (planned). This is the stronger check: take the approved proposals, apply them to the same starting tree on another machine, and compare. Current records what makes that comparison exact. Each edit stores the file's before and after content hashes, and each command stores its exit code and output, so a re-run can be diffed against the original byte for byte. Edits replay deterministically. Commands are as reproducible as the environment they run in, and a difference shows up as a different artifact hash. A current export / current replay pair to do this is on the roadmap. Verifiability: a hash-chained history The commit log is a hash chain, the structure blockchains use to make history tamper-evident (without mining, tokens or multi-party consensus). commit 1 commit 2 commit 3 ┌────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │ index: 1 │ │ index: 2 │ │ index: 3 │ │ previous: nil │◀───│ previous: H(c1) │◀───│ previous: H(c2) │◀── head │ events: [...] │ │ events: [...] │ │ events: [...] │ └────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ H(c) = SHA-256 of term_to_binary(commit, [:deterministic]) Changing any byte of any past commit changes its hash and breaks every link after it, so the head hash fingerprints the entire history. It also covers the content: events refer to file contents, edits, command output and model replies by their SHA-256 artifact ids, so those are committed to as well. Only valid successors are written. A commit must have the next index and the head's hash as previous_hash, or it is refused and nothing is written. Durable before acknowledged. A commit is fsynced before anyone hears of it. Verified on every start. Every link is re-checked, across segments. A gap, a broken link or corrupt bytes stop the runtime from starting, naming the file. It refuses to serve a history it can't vouch for. Closed segments are immutable, and opened read-only. Commit hashes currently use :erlang.term_to_binary/2 with the :deterministic option. This makes term encoding deterministic within the supported Erlang term format, but does not guarantee byte-for-byte identical encoding across OTP versions. Cross-version verification needs a stable, versioned canonical encoding (see the roadmap). What this proves today: integrity. The history the runtime replays is exactly the history it wrote, unbroken and in order. What it doesn't yet: authenticity to an outsider. Commits aren't signed, so someone who can write the data directory can rewrite history and recompute every hash. Signing the head, or publishing it somewhere the writer can't reach, closes that gap: once a third party holds a head hash, every request, approval and effect beneath it is verifiable against it. That, and re-verifying artifact hashes on read, are on the roadmap. Architecture Current applies functional-programming and distributed-systems patterns to agent workflows. Each provides one of the properties above. Pattern In Current Gives you Event sourcing Every step is a typed, past-tense, versioned event. The log is the only source of truth Provenance, replay CQRS Commands (submit, approve, revise, apply) go through Current.API and become proposed events. Queries read projections (WorkflowStore, ProposalStore, TaskStore) built from committed events Reads never mutate; writes are only events Pure reducer WorkflowReducer.apply_event/2: state × event → state, or refusal Deterministic state; one definition of what is allowed Immutability Events are never edited or deleted; corrections are new events. Artifacts never change A history worth verifying Content addressing Artifacts are named by the SHA-256 of their bytes Deduplication, and content that checks itself Hash-chained WAL Each commit carries the previous commit's hash Tamper evidence Interpreter pattern Intents are data in a closed algebra; EffectApplicator is the one module that interprets them against the world The agent can't act; a minimal trusted surface Pure core, impure edge Model calls and effects run at the edge and come back as events Effects are captured, not hidden Schema evolution by upcasting Old events are migrated on read by pure, versioned functions, never rewritten on disk Old logs keep replaying through new code Consensus interface Commits are ordered through Current.Consensus.propose/1; single-node today A path to a replicated log The reducer At the center is one pure function: WorkflowReducer.apply_event(workflow | nil, event) :: {:ok, workflow} | {:error, {:invalid_transition, status, event_type}} WorkflowReducer.replay(events) # a fold of apply_event over the log It reads no clock, touches no disk and calls no model. Every timestamp comes from the event. It is the workflow state machine, an explicit table of (status, event) → status clauses, and anything not in the table is refused: Rule Enforced by Nothing applies without approval EffectApplicationStarted is accepted only from :approved A plan can never be applied ProposalApproved is accepted only for mode: :apply One decision per proposal approval, rejection and a revision request are accepted only from :waiting_for_approval Only the latest proposal can be decided approval, rejection, a revision request and EffectApplicationStarted must name the workflow's most recent proposal, else {:stale_proposal, given, current} Revisions are bounded a revision request is refused with {:revision_limit_reached, max} once max_revisions (recorded on WorkflowCreated, default 10) are used Terminal means terminal nothing moves a completed, planned, rejected, failed or abandoned workflow The same function is used at every layer, so the layers can't disagree. EventStore replays a workflow's events plus each new one at commit time, so an event the reducer refuses never becomes canonical, and of two racing approvals only one is accepted. The API runs it as an early check before proposing. The projections are the reducer applied to the stream, and recovery replays through it on restart. Because acceptance is itself a pure function of the events already accepted, replaying the log reproduces every rejection as well as every state. The orchestrator is a policy, not a script WorkflowOrchestrator maps each committed event to the next event it proposes (WorkflowCreated → ProposalProductionStarted, ProposalProduced → ProposalValidated | ProposalValidationFailed, ...). It never changes state directly, and acts only on what is committed. Model calls and effects run in separate processes, and their results come back as messages that become events. Nothing an effect does counts until it is an event. Never guess after a crash On restart, every workflow is rebuilt from the log and resumed from what the log says. A workflow interrupted mid-apply is failed rather than resumed, because an effect that may already have happened is never repeated. One that crash-loops is retried with backoff, then abandoned on the record. Intents Intent What it does when applied Allowed in observe read_file Reads a file and stores its contents yes glob Lists files matching a relative pattern yes grep Finds lines containing a literal string in listed files yes write_file Creates a new file; fails if it already exists edit_file Replaces exact text (old_string → new_string); must match once unless replace_all; stores before and after delete_file Deletes a file; stores its contents first run_command Runs an executable with arguments in the project; stores stdout, stderr and exit code claim Checks a statement against an earlier intent's result (exit_code_equals, match_count_equals, match_count_greater_than) report A summary for the reader; no effect CLI reference Command What it does current run <prompt> --model <m> [--dir <d>] [--timeout-minutes <n>] Make a request; stops when the proposal waits for review. current plan <prompt> --model <m> [--dir <d>] [--timeout-minutes <n>] Produce and validate a proposal that can never be applied. current review <proposal-id> [--json] [--max-lines <n>] [--raw] A proposal with its edits, files and commands. --json emits current.review/v1. current approve <proposal-id> [-m <message>] Record approval. Nothing is applied. current reject <proposal-id> [-m <message>] Turn a proposal down; the workflow ends. current revise <proposal-id> -m <feedback> Send a proposal back. The agent produces a replacement; follows the workflow until it waits for review again. Must name the latest proposal. current apply <proposal-id> Apply an approved proposal, verify its claims, follow it to the end. current events <workflow-or-task-id> The chain: a workflow's events, in log order. current proposal <proposal-id> A proposal in full: intents, claims, observations, artifacts. current artifact <artifact-id> An artifact's exact bytes, for piping. current models Models discovered from the configured providers. current status Whether the runtime is up, and how it is configured. --model is required; use a name current models prints. --timeout-minutes is 1 to 60. The CLI holds no state: interrupt it at any point and the workflow carries on in the runtime. Exit codes are 0 on the expected outcome, 1 on failure and 2 on a usage error. HTTP API The CLI does nothing a script, or another agent, can't: it calls these routes. Route Does POST /v1/tasks Submit a task: {"prompt", "model", "dir", "mode", "timeout_ms"} → 202 {"task_id"} GET /v1/workflows/:id A workflow's status and events (a task id or unique prefix works) GET /v1/workflows/:id/activity What the model has asked to see so far (?epoch=&after_seq=) GET /v1/proposals/:id A proposal in full GET /v1/proposals/:id/review The current.review/v1 document (?max_lines=&raw=true) POST /v1/proposals/:id/approve Record approval: {"message", "reviewed_by"} POST /v1/proposals/:id/reject Turn the proposal down POST /v1/proposals/:id/revise Send it back: {"feedback", "reviewed_by"}. 409 stale_proposal if a newer proposal exists (details.current_proposal_id); 409 revision_limit_reached when none are left POST /v1/proposals/:id/apply Start applying an approved proposal GET /v1/artifacts/:id An artifact's exact bytes GET /v1/models, GET /v1/health The model catalog; whether the runtime is up Errors are {"error": {"code", "message"}} with a matching status. The API does no authentication (see Security). Every route checks Host and, when present, Origin before reading the body. Loopback Host values must use the configured runtime port; deployments behind another hostname must add its exact authority to http[:allowed_hosts]. MCP Current also exposes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at POST /mcp, using Streamable HTTP and protocol version 2025-06-18. It exposes tools for submitting tasks, inspecting workflows and proposals, reviewing and retrieving artifacts, approving, rejecting, requesting revisions, applying proposals, listing models, and checking runtime health. The MCP endpoint uses the same Current.API and runtime invariants as the CLI and HTTP API. Tasks return immediately with a task id; clients poll get_workflow for progress. It is stateless and tools-only: no sessions, resources, prompts, server-initiated streams, or batch requests. GET /mcp is not supported. MCP does not authenticate callers. Anyone who can reach the endpoint can submit, approve, and apply proposals. Keep it on loopback or behind a trusted gateway that enforces access control. Like every route, it checks Host and Origin; it additionally checks MCP-Protocol-Version and Content-Type. These are not substitutes for authentication. See Security and the threat model. Configuration Environment Variable Read by Meaning OPENAI_API_KEY runtime Enables openai:* models ANTHROPIC_API_KEY runtime Enables anthropic:* models CURRENT_DATA_DIR runtime (prod) Where the log and artifacts live (default ./_data) CURRENT_ALLOWED_COMMANDS runtime Comma-separated exact cmd values allowed for run_command; unset keeps the configured default CURRENT_HTTP_PORT runtime Port of the HTTP API (default 4000) CURRENT_HTTP_IP runtime Address the HTTP API binds (default 127.0.0.1) CURRENT_URL CLI Where the CLI finds the runtime (default http://127.0.0.1:4000) The runtime starts without an API key, but its model catalog is empty until one is set. Application config (config/*.exs) Key Default Meaning data_dir "./_data" Log in consensus/, artifacts in artifacts/ generate_proposal_files false (true in dev) Write a Markdown snapshot of each produced proposal under <data_dir>/proposals/ allowed_commands [] Executables run_command may run; empty denies all. The configured list is included in the model prompt. Not a sandbox llm_proposal_timeout_ms 240_000 Bound on one model call llm_task_timeout_ms 600_000 Default bound on producing one proposal commit_log_segment_bytes 64 MiB Log segment size before rolling over proposal_builder Current.LLMProposalBuilder What produces proposals effect_applicator Current.EffectApplicator What applies intents http[:allowed_hosts] [] Exact Host authorities allowed in addition to loopback hosts on the configured port, for example current.internal:443 mcp[:allowed_origins] [] Exact browser origins allowed on every route in addition to loopback origins mcp[:allow_loopback_origins] true Whether browser origins on localhost, 127.0.0.1, and [::1] are accepted model_catalog_clients OpenAI, Anthropic Providers asked for models Proposal snapshots. When generate_proposal_files is true, the runtime periodically writes a human-readable Markdown snapshot of each produced proposal to <data_dir>/proposals/<timestamp>-<task-slug>-<id>/r<revision>-<id>.md. They are a convenience for reading proposals outside the CLI and are regenerated from the log if missing. It is enabled in config/dev.exs and disabled by default. Snapshots can contain sensitive project content (file contents, diffs and commands), so treat them like the rest of the data directory. Security Current controls when an agent's proposal takes effect and records everything about it. It does not limit what an approved proposal can do. Nothing an agent proposes runs without approval and a separate apply, enforced by the reducer at commit time. Paths are confined to the project, checked lexically at validation and again, following symlinks, just before each effect. What the model sees is filtered by name (dependencies, build output, VCS directories, .env*). Other secrets in the project are not recognised. run_command is restricted by an exact executable allowlist, not sandboxed. Commands are denied by default. The proposal's cmd must exactly match a configured entry; a bare name is resolved on PATH, while a relative path containing / is resolved from the project. Allowed commands run through a Bash wrapper in the project directory with the runtime's privileges and inherited environment, including filesystem and network access. Arguments are unrestricted, so allowing interpreters, shells, package managers, or script-dispatching executables can permit arbitrary code execution. There is currently no command timeout, output-size cap, environment allowlist, or explicit descendant-process cleanup. Output is captured in unbounded temporary files until the command exits. The HTTP API is unauthenticated. It listens on 127.0.0.1. Every route validates Host and browser Origin to prevent DNS rebinding, but these checks do not authenticate non-browser clients. Restrict who can reach it with a gateway, proxy or network policy; anyone who can reach it can approve and apply. The log is tamper-evident to the runtime, not yet to an attacker. See Verifiability. Full analysis: docs/threat_model.md. Please report vulnerabilities privately. linked in one log ✅ What the model read, and its raw replies, recorded with the proposal ✅ Verified claims: a false claim fails the workflow ✅ Pure reducer enforcing every transition at commit time ✅ Hash-chained, segmented WAL, verified on every start ✅ State and rejections rebuilt deterministically from the log ✅ Content-addressed artifacts for every input and output ✅ Versioned events with upcasting ✅ OpenAI and Anthropic models, chosen per task ✅ MCP tools over stateless Streamable HTTP (POST /mcp) ✅ Command executable allowlist (deny by default) ✅ current export / current replay: re-execute on another machine and diff planned current verify: check the chain and every artifact, print the head hash planned Signed or externally anchored log heads planned Approval policy hook / authenticated approvers planned (layered on top) Command timeout, output cap, environment filtering, and process-tree cleanup planned Atomic apply, simulate planned Roadmap Next current export and current replay: bundle a workflow's events and artifacts, re-apply on another machine against the same starting tree, and diff every artifact hash current verify: re-check the chain and every artifact against its name, and print the head hash an approval policy hook (N approvers, an approver other than the requester), where an ACL layer plugs in command timeout, output cap, environment filtering, and process-tree cleanup atomic apply, and simulate in a throwaway copy Later signed log heads, and publishing head hashes externally a stable, versioned canonical encoding for commit hashes (today they use :erlang.term_to_binary([:deterministic]), which does not guarantee identical bytes across OTP versions) log snapshots, so startup doesn't replay everything sandboxed interpreters a replicated content_html_zh:
Change control for AI agents

Agents propose changes. Current validates them, waits for your approval, applies them, and records every step in a tamper-evident log.

The Elevator Pitch · See it in action · Quickstart · How it works · Provenance · Reproducibility · Verifiability · Architecture · Intents · CLI · HTTP API · MCP · Configuration · Security · Status · Roadmap

The Elevator Pitch

Why not just use Claude Code or Codex? 你可以。 But there, the agent acts and you approve step by step as it goes. In Current, the agent can’t act at all. It hands over a complete proposal, and nothing happens until that proposal is approved and applied.

  • Safety: The agent is limited to doing just one thing -- producing proposals. It sees only the files it asks for that Current's read policy permits, and can only propose changes from nine typed intents. Nothing touches your project until you approve it, and only allowlisted commands can run.
  • Verification: You don’t take the agent’s word for it. You review the exact proposal, or have other agents review it, before anything happens, and Current checks the agent’s claims against what actually ran.
  • Provenance: As agents write more of the code, someone will ask why was this changed, and who approved it? Current answers from a commit log: the oldest, best-tested idea in systems.

That log is hash-chained, so changes to past history are detectable, and the full state can be rebuilt from it on another machine.

Status: early. Single node, local projects. Current is not a sandbox or an authentication system: approved commands run with the runtime's privileges. See Security and the threat model.

查看实际效果

Ask Current to add CSRF protection to the included Next.js example:

current run "add CSRF protection to this app" \
  --dir examples/nextjs-auth \
  --model openai:gpt-5.6-sol

The model never gets the repository. It sees the layout and asks for what it needs, and Current fetches each file:

… round 1: the model asked to see 8 things
    ✓ read_file app/api/login/route.ts       769 B
    ✓ read_file lib/auth.ts                  626 B
    ✓ read_file lib/rate-limit.ts            2.4 KB
    ✓ read_file tests/login.test.ts          847 B
    ✓ read_file tests/rate-limit.test.ts     2.3 KB
    ✓ read_file package.json                 343 B
    ✓ read_file tsconfig.json                221 B
    ✓ read_file .gitignore                   83 B

Reads are confined to the project. Dependencies, build output, .git and .env* files are never shown to the model, and every read is recorded.

Then it returns a proposal:

Agent produced proposal
  proposal sha256:672c4973787b…

  The login route already invokes a missing CSRF validator before parsing
  credentials. Implement that validator with fail-closed same-origin Origin
  checking and add focused coverage for accepted and rejected origins.

PROPOSED

   1  WriteFile    lib/csrf.ts
   2  WriteFile    tests/csrf.test.ts
   3  RunCommand   npm test
   4  Report       Add fail-closed same-origin CSRF validation for the login
                   route and unit tests covering valid, absent, malformed,
                   and cross-origin headers.

✓ Proposal decoded
✓ Proposal validated

Waiting for approval. Nothing has been applied.

The agent has proposed a change. Your project is untouched.

Review the exact files and commands, or pass the machine-readable version (--json) to another agent for a second opinion:

current review sha256:672c4973787b

Then decide. Send it back with feedback, and the model reads more and returns a new proposal:

current revise sha256:672c4973787b -m "add a test for a missing Origin header"

Or approve it. Approval is recorded, but nothing runs yet:

current approve sha256:672c4973787b -m "LGTM"
✓ Approved sha256:672c4973787b
  message  LGTM

Nothing has been applied. Apply it with:
  current apply sha256:672c4973787b

Applying is its own step. Current, not the agent, writes the files and runs the command:

current apply sha256:672c4973787b
✓ Proposal approved
✓ Workflow completed

MODE: APPLY
4 effects executed.

Inspect
  current events   sha256:1429719b7546
  current proposal sha256:672c4973787b
  current artifact sha256:fb30687f1722   (raw model output)

Every step above, from the request and each file the model read to its raw reply, the approval and each effect's output, is now part of the workflow's record. current events prints it.

快速入门

要求

  • Elixir 1.19 on Erlang/OTP (mise.toml pins OTP 28.5 and Elixir 1.19.5; run mise install if you use mise)
  • git, make, and bash
  • An OpenAI or Anthropic API key

1. Get the code and build

git clone https://github.com/santosh79/current.git
cd current
mix deps.get
mix compile
make client

2. Start the runtime

In one terminal, export a key and start the server. It listens on 127.0.0.1:4000 and prints every request and commit as it happens.

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="..."     # or OPENAI_API_KEY
export CURRENT_ALLOWED_COMMANDS=npm  # commands are denied unless allowlisted
bin/current-server

3. 提出请求

In another terminal, from the repository root:

export PATH="$PWD:$PATH"   # puts the local `current` CLI on PATH
current models             # the models your keys give you
MODEL="openai:gpt-5.6"     # replace with a model listed above

current run "add CSRF protection to this app" \
  --dir examples/nextjs-auth \
  --model $MODEL

run stops when the proposal is waiting for review. Output varies between models and runs. Use plan instead of run for a proposal that can be reviewed but never applied.

4. Review, decide, apply

current review  <proposal-id>
current revise  <proposal-id> -m "keep the route check, add edge cases"
current approve <proposal-id> -m "reviewed"
current apply   <proposal-id>

Or current reject <proposal-id> -m "..." to end the workflow. A revision produces a new proposal ID, which must be reviewed and approved in turn; the earlier one is stale. IDs can be shortened to a unique prefix of at least four hex characters.

5. Trace it

current events   <workflow-id>   # the full chain, in log order
current proposal <proposal-id>   # intents, claims, and what the model read
current artifact <artifact-id>   # exact bytes: a file, command output, a raw reply

它是如何运作的

In a typical agent, a tool call is the action: the file is written the moment the model decides to write it. In Current, the model's output is a proposal, a list of typed intents:

"in lib/signup.ex, replace this text with that"; "run mix test"; "claim the tests pass, because that command exits 0"

A proposal does nothing on its own. Between it and your project, the runtime:

  1. decodes the model's reply, which is untrusted bytes, into a closed set of intent types. Anything outside it is rejected, not interpreted;
  2. validates it: paths confined to the project, files exist, every edit matches exactly, claims cite earlier intents they can be checked against;
  3. waits for a decision. A proposal is reviewed as a unit and approved, rejected, or sent back with feedback. The reviewer can be a person or another agent: each decision is an API call, recorded as its own event with the reviewer's metadata. A decision must name the workflow's latest proposal, and revisions are bounded (10 by default);
  4. applies it, in a separate step, with a small trusted interpreter that re-checks every path immediately before touching it and records every result;
  5. checks the outcome itself. Claims are evaluated against recorded results, and a claim that doesn't hold fails the workflow.

Every step is an event. Rounded boxes are where a workflow ends.

Producing a proposal

  1. A task is submitted with a prompt, a project directory and a model. The directory is resolved once to its real path and recorded.
  2. The model is given the project's layout: paths and sizes, no contents. Dependencies, build output, VCS directories and .env* files are left out.
  3. The model may reply with an observe request: up to 20 read_file, glob or grep intents, each with a reason. The runtime runs them read-only, under path confinement and the read policy, and asks again with the results. Up to 8 rounds, 400 KB of results in total, 200 KB per file.
  4. The model replies with a proposal. Its exact reply is stored as an artifact, whatever it contains.
  5. The proposal is decoded into typed intents (wire contract), every path is made absolute against the project, and it is validated.

Validation answers "is this well-formed and in bounds right now?", not "will it apply cleanly?". The project can change before apply, and those failures are caught and recorded then. Producing a proposal is bounded by llm_proposal_timeout_ms per call and the task's --timeout-minutes (default 10) overall.

Applying it

apply starts the interpreter. It re-checks every path against the filesystem as it is now (following symlinks), then carries out the intents in order. The first failure, or the first claim that doesn't hold, stops it and fails the workflow. Effects are not rolled back. The re-check narrows the window for a path to escape the project but doesn't close it (T2 in the threat model).

生命周期

created → planning → validating → waiting_for_approval
   plan mode:   → planned
   apply mode:  → approved → applying → assembling_result → completed
                → rejected
                → revision_requested → planning → validating → waiting_for_approval
                  (bounded; each pass adds a proposal to the workflow)
any stage:      → failed      (production, validation or an effect failed)
                → abandoned   (no further automatic progress is possible)
planning:  the model sees the layout, may ask to read files, then returns a proposal

Three primitives

Primitive When Role More
Intent Before execution A proposal, as data intent.md
Event After execution or decision A fact event.md
人工制品 Throughout Immutable bytes, named by their SHA-256 artifact.md
Intents propose change. Artifacts hold bytes. Events record fact. State is derived from the event log.

Provenance: from a change back to the request

Because the runtime is the only thing that acts, and records each step before taking the next, every change sits at the end of an explicit chain:

TaskCreated                  the request: prompt, model, project, submitted_at
└─ WorkflowCreated
   └─ ProposalProduced       intents, what the model read first, its raw reply
      └─ ProposalValidated
         ├─ ProposalRevisionRequested   who asked for what change; loops back to
         │  └─ ProposalProductionStarted → ProposalProduced (revision 1, revises
         │     the one above) → ProposalValidated → ... up to the bound
         └─ ProposalApproved     who, when, with what message
            └─ EffectApplicationStarted
               ├─ EffectApplied      an edit: file before and after
               ├─ EffectApplied      a command: exit code, stdout, stderr
               ├─ EffectApplied      a claim: verified, and against what
               └─ WorkflowCompleted

So for any change you can answer, from the record alone and without the model:

问题 Answered by
Who asked for this, and what exactly did they ask? TaskCreated: the prompt, model and project
Why does the agent say it's needed? The proposal's justification and claims
What did the model look at before deciding? Each observation, with its reason and the exact bytes it was shown
What did the model actually say? Its raw reply, stored byte for byte
Who authorized it, and when? ProposalApproved and its metadata
What did the reviewer ask to change, and what came of it? ProposalRevisionRequested and the next proposal's revision and revises
What exactly changed? Each effect's result: file before and after, command output
Did it do what the agent claimed? Each claim's verification and evidence
What didn't happen, and why? Rejections, validation failures, failed effects, each with a reason

Authorization is recorded, not enforced by identity. Current guarantees that nothing is applied without an approval event in the chain, followed by a separate apply, and the reducer enforces that at commit time. Who may approve is for a layer in front of it: approvals enter through one route (POST /v1/proposals/:id/approve), where a gateway can authenticate the caller and write verified identity into the approval's metadata. Today reviewed_by is whatever the client sends.

Reproducibility: replay the record anywhere

The commit log and the artifact store are the whole of Current's state. Nothing else is persisted, and everything the runtime shows you (tasks, proposals, workflows) is rebuilt from them. So the record is portable: copy the data directory to another machine, and replaying it gives the same history.

There are two levels of replay, and it matters which one you mean.

Replaying the record (works today). Every workflow state is a pure function of its events (see the reducer). Every piece of content those events refer to is an immutable artifact named by its SHA-256. Replaying the same log, anywhere, gives the same states, the same accepted transitions and the same rejections, and every artifact can be checked against its own name. Point CURRENT_DATA_DIR at a copy and the runtime rebuilds it on start. (Starting the runtime also resumes or fails workflows that were still in progress, which appends new events. Copy a record whose workflows have finished.)

Re-executing the proposals (planned). This is the stronger check: take the approved proposals, apply them to the same starting tree on another machine, and compare. Current records what makes that comparison exact. Each edit stores the file's before and after content hashes, and each command stores its exit code and output, so a re-run can be diffed against the original byte for byte. Edits replay deterministically. Commands are as reproducible as the environment they run in, and a difference shows up as a different artifact hash. A current export / current replay pair to do this is on the roadmap.

Verifiability: a hash-chained history

The commit log is a hash chain, the structure blockchains use to make history tamper-evident (without mining, tokens or multi-party consensus).

commit 1              commit 2                commit 3
┌────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐
│ index: 1       │    │ index: 2         │    │ index: 3         │
│ previous: nil  │◀───│ previous: H(c1)  │◀───│ previous: H(c2)  │◀── head
│ events: [...]  │    │ events: [...]    │    │ events: [...]    │
└────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘
                 H(c) = SHA-256 of term_to_binary(commit, [:deterministic])

Changing any byte of any past commit changes its hash and breaks every link after it, so the head hash fingerprints the entire history. It also covers the content: events refer to file contents, edits, command output and model replies by their SHA-256 artifact ids, so those are committed to as well.

  • Only valid successors are written. A commit must have the next index and the head's hash as previous_hash, or it is refused and nothing is written.
  • Durable before acknowledged. A commit is fsynced before anyone hears of it.
  • Verified on every start. Every link is re-checked, across segments. A gap, a broken link or corrupt bytes stop the runtime from starting, naming the file. It refuses to serve a history it can't vouch for.
  • Closed segments are immutable, and opened read-only.

Commit hashes currently use :erlang.term_to_binary/2 with the :deterministic option. This makes term encoding deterministic within the supported Erlang term format, but does not guarantee byte-for-byte identical encoding across OTP versions. Cross-version verification needs a stable, versioned canonical encoding (see the roadmap).

What this proves today: integrity. The history the runtime replays is exactly the history it wrote, unbroken and in order. What it doesn't yet: authenticity to an outsider. Commits aren't signed, so someone who can write the data directory can rewrite history and recompute every hash. Signing the head, or publishing it somewhere the writer can't reach, closes that gap: once a third party holds a head hash, every request, approval and effect beneath it is verifiable against it. That, and re-verifying artifact hashes on read, are on the roadmap.

The reducer

At the center is one pure function:

WorkflowReducer.apply_event(workflow | nil, event)
  :: {:ok, workflow} | {:error, {:invalid_transition, status, event_type}}

WorkflowReducer.replay(events)   # a fold of apply_event over the log

It reads no clock, touches no disk and calls no model. Every timestamp comes from the event. It is the workflow state machine, an explicit table of (status, event) → status clauses, and anything not in the table is refused:

Rule Enforced by
Nothing applies without approval EffectApplicationStarted is accepted only from :approved
A plan can never be applied ProposalApproved is accepted only for mode: :apply
One decision per proposal approval, rejection and a revision request are accepted only from :waiting_for_approval
Only the latest proposal can be decided approval, rejection, a revision request and EffectApplicationStarted must name the workflow's most recent proposal, else {:stale_proposal, given, current}
Revisions are bounded a revision request is refused with {:revision_limit_reached, max} once max_revisions (recorded on WorkflowCreated, default 10) are used
Terminal means terminal nothing moves a completed, planned, rejected, failed or abandoned workflow

The same function is used at every layer, so the layers can't disagree. EventStore replays a workflow's events plus each new one at commit time, so an event the reducer refuses never becomes canonical, and of two racing approvals only one is accepted. The API runs it as an early check before proposing. The projections are the reducer applied to the stream, and recovery replays through it on restart. Because acceptance is itself a pure function of the events already accepted, replaying the log reproduces every rejection as well as every state.

The orchestrator is a policy, not a script

WorkflowOrchestrator maps each committed event to the next event it proposes (WorkflowCreated → ProposalProductionStarted, ProposalProduced → ProposalValidated | ProposalValidationFailed, ...). It never changes state directly, and acts only on what is committed. Model calls and effects run in separate processes, and their results come back as messages that become events. Nothing an effect does counts until it is an event.

Never guess after a crash

On restart, every workflow is rebuilt from the log and resumed from what the log says. A workflow interrupted mid-apply is failed rather than resumed, because an effect that may already have happened is never repeated. One that crash-loops is retried with backoff, then abandoned on the record.

MCP

Current also exposes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at POST /mcp, using Streamable HTTP and protocol version 2025-06-18. It exposes tools for submitting tasks, inspecting workflows and proposals, reviewing and retrieving artifacts, approving, rejecting, requesting revisions, applying proposals, listing models, and checking runtime health.

The MCP endpoint uses the same Current.API and runtime invariants as the CLI and HTTP API. Tasks return immediately with a task id; clients poll get_workflow for progress. It is stateless and tools-only: no sessions, resources, prompts, server-initiated streams, or batch requests. GET /mcp is not supported.

MCP does not authenticate callers. Anyone who can reach the endpoint can submit, approve, and apply proposals. Keep it on loopback or behind a trusted gateway that enforces access control. Like every route, it checks Host and Origin; it additionally checks MCP-Protocol-Version and Content-Type. These are not substitutes for authentication. See Security and the threat model.

安全

Current controls when an agent's proposal takes effect and records everything about it. It does not limit what an approved proposal can do.

  • Nothing an agent proposes runs without approval and a separate apply, enforced by the reducer at commit time.
  • Paths are confined to the project, checked lexically at validation and again, following symlinks, just before each effect.
  • What the model sees is filtered by name (dependencies, build output, VCS directories, .env*). Other secrets in the project are not recognised.
  • run_command is restricted by an exact executable allowlist, not sandboxed. Commands are denied by default. The proposal's cmd must exactly match a configured entry; a bare name is resolved on PATH, while a relative path containing / is resolved from the project. Allowed commands run through a Bash wrapper in the project directory with the runtime's privileges and inherited environment, including filesystem and network access. Arguments are unrestricted, so allowing interpreters, shells, package managers, or script-dispatching executables can permit arbitrary code execution. There is currently no command timeout, output-size cap, environment allowlist, or explicit descendant-process cleanup. Output is captured in unbounded temporary files until the command exits.
  • The HTTP API is unauthenticated. It listens on 127.0.0.1. Every route validates Host and browser Origin to prevent DNS rebinding, but these checks do not authenticate non-browser clients. Restrict who can reach it with a gateway, proxy or network policy; anyone who can reach it can approve and apply.
  • The log is tamper-evident to the runtime, not yet to an attacker. See Verifiability.
